newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Floods hamper Czech economy, full impact unclear.
newsitem.headline: Floods hamper Czech economy, full impact unclear.

text.p: The entire Czech economy is expected to take a mild to moderate hit from recent flooding in the east, but the impact should be somewhat tempered by reconstruction in the area, analysts said on Thursday.

Prague's Komercni Banka said the floods, which submerged low-lying areas after torrential rains last week killing 46 people, should keep 1997 gross domestic product growth at the bottom of their forecast range of 1.5-2.5 percent.
"The drop in production in the flooded territories will lead to a very low GDP figure for the third quarter of 1997," Komercni's Chief Economist Kamil Janacek told reporters.

"Reconstruction and renewal works however will lead to both an increase in the growth rate of investment into fixed capital and to a milder drop in public consumption than previously expected," he added.
The worst flooding of the century forced scores of road and rail links to be cut and hundreds of businesses, including major factories, to shut production.

Hundreds of farms, houses and apartment buildings in major population centres such as Olomouc and Ostrava were destroyed. Total damage estimates range from 50 to 100 billion crowns ($1.45 billion to $2.9 billion), and more rain is forecast for the saturated area this weekend.
"It's certain the impact on GDP will not be neutral but it cannot be said...how the factors will come together," Industry and Trade Minister Karel Kuehnl told a news conference.

Komercni said it expected that -- after adjusting for the floods' impact -- average inflation for 1997 should be about 10 percent, rising to as much as 12 percent in 1998 as the impact of higher interest rates and a weaker crown bites.
June inflation was 6.8 percent, year-on-year.
The bank said unemployment would rise to 4.5-4.7 percent by the end of the year, from 4.4 in June. Losses to the industrial sector alone should total over 10 billion crowns.

"The floods are very unfortunate, not only for people of those areas, but also for the whole macro-economy," said Vladimir Kreidl, economist at Patria Finance. "Expenditures (for reconstruction) are understandibly needed, but the question is where will (the money) come from," he added.
The government, already stung by a huge trade deficit which forced budget cuts to slow demand and defend the weakened crown, earmarked about 11 billion crowns for flood relief.
The money will be provided from a combination of up to five billion crowns in domestic bond issues and proceeds drawn from state assets such as receipts from privatisation.
On Thursday, Finance Minister Ivan Pilip said talks have begun with the European Investment Bank on an infrastructure reconstruction loan exceeding 10 billion crowns.
Komercni's Janacek suggested that the country could live with a higher strain on the money supply for a while.

"Companies this year have lived through several shocks when the volume of money (supply growth rate) in the economy throughout the year fell by more than half," Janacek said. "My proposal is to allow money supply growth of up to the level of nominal GDP growth, meaning an inflationary 12 percent."

The central bank, which has been fighting the twin battles of defending the Czech crown and reducing inflation while trying to keep the economy moving, has been criticised by some government officials for an excessively tight monetary policy.

The central bank recently has been lowering interbank interest rates since raising them to prohibitive levels during the May attack on the crown, but has given no indication that a deeper easing in monetary policy is on the cards.
Patria's Kreidl, however, bristled at Janacek's suggestion.
"There isn't room for further expenditure in the economy. An increase in taxes may be considered so that it eases the pressure on monetary policy," Kreidl said.
-- Prague Newsroom, 420-2-2423-0003 ($ = 34.18 Czech Crowns)
